You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.
(One of the texts is a real LinkedIn post by a person, written on its own topic; judge tells, not topic.)

=== TEXT A ===
Many PMs fail a job interview due to a product vision.

Yet, it is easy to understand.

Leading a product without a clear vision is like walking through a foreign city without a map. You might be moving, but you are going nowhere.

A product vision describes the overarching long-term mission of your product. Vision statements are aspirational and communicate concisely where the product hopes to go and what it hopes to achieve in the long term.

Effective vision needs to be:

✅ Inspiring — people who help to implement the vision should feel inspired.

✅ Achievable — it must have a decent chance to work. Don't dream of traveling to Alpha Centauri until you send humans to Mars.

✅ Documented — do not let the vision stay in your head. You actually need to write it to make it work.

✅ Communicated — it seems obvious, yet many forget about this. Vision will only work if you tell others about it.

✅ Emotional — vision becomes much more memorable when others can imagine themselves doing something practical and when it speaks to their hearts.

My favorite example of the vision is president John F. Kennedy's vision of space exploration (below).

Be patient, as creating the product vision is not a one-time task. You have to communicate with others, get feedback and adapt. Your product vision will emerge and evolve over time.

How does it connect to a product strategy? 

I'll describe it Tomorrow.

#productmanagement #agile

=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
We spent three months building a feature nobody asked for.

It started the way these things always start. A few power users mentioned something adjacent in a support ticket. Someone sketched a mock in a meeting. Suddenly we had a Jira epic, a design sprint, and a Slack channel with 40 people in it.

The feature was beautiful. Edge cases handled. Analytics instrumented. Launch post drafted. We even named it.

Week one after ship: 12 users tried it.
Week two: 4.
Week four: 1, and I think it was me checking that it still worked.

Nobody complained. Nobody filed bugs. They just… didn’t care. The problem we solved was real for us. It was almost imaginary for them.

Here’s what I got wrong, and what I’d do differently.

I confused internal conviction with user demand. We were solving our own frustration with the product, then projecting it onto customers. “If we need this, they must need it too” is not research. It’s autobiography.

I treated discovery as a phase we had already finished. We talked to users—just not about this. We assumed adjacent pain meant this solution. We never put a prototype in front of five people and asked them to complete a real task. We never asked what they would stop doing if this existed. We never asked what they already used instead.

I optimized for completeness over learning. We built the full version because shipping “half” felt unprofessional. In reality, the unprofessional thing was spending a quarter on an untested bet. A weekend prototype and a dozen conversations would have killed it—or reshaped it—before we wrote production code.

The feature is gone now. We turned it off. The code is still in the repo like a monument to a meeting that went too well.

The lesson I keep: shipping is not validation. Usage is. Before the epic, write the smallest thing that could prove someone would miss it if it disappeared. If you can’t get that signal, you don’t have a feature. You have a story you told yourselves.

Talk to users about the job, not your idea. Watch what they already do. Build less, sooner. And if the room is excited and the customers are quiet—believe the quiet.

What’s a feature you shipped that taught you the same thing the hard way?
=== END OF TEXT B ===

tells_A: 5. Bulleted list with bold lead-ins and checkmark emojis
tells_B: 1. Negative parallelism repeated heavily ('is not research. It’s autobiography', 'shipping is not validation. Usage is', 'you don’t have a feature. You have a story you told yourselves', 'Talk to users about the job, not your idea')
2. Signposting ('Here’s what I got wrong, and what I’d do differently')
6. Triadic sentence structures and lists of three ('a Jira epic, a design sprint, and a Slack channel', three consecutive 'We never...' sentences, 'Talk... Watch... Build...')
9. Relentless short punchy fragments and uniform LinkedIn cadence
13. Frequent em dashes used as default joints ('users—just', 'killed it—or reshaped it—before', 'quiet—believe')
16. Generic manufactured anecdote with vague non-specifics ('a feature nobody asked for', no domain, no product name)
